message.content:
You are doing an ADVERSARIAL SECURITY REVIEW of Nxeon's shared-hosting feature (many customers isolated on one Linux box via jailed unix users + per-user PHP-FPM pools + nginx name-based vhosts + scoped MySQL users) at /opt/nxeon. This gates whether the owner can safely sell shared hosting to real paying customers.

Your LENS: privilege escalation and cross-tenant breakout — can Tenant A ever read/write Tenant B's files, databases, or processes, or escalate to root on the shared node? Assume the attacker is a malicious PAYING customer with full SSH/SFTP access to their own jailed account, full control of their own PHP code, their own cron jobs, and full access to the in-portal DB Studio query tool — NOT an anonymous outsider. What's the worst they can do from inside their own sandbox?

Files to review closely:
- worker/hosting.ts (the provisioner: vhost/FPM pool generation, cron writing, backup/restore, subdomain/addon-domain creation, DB creation, lifecycle SUSPEND/UNSUSPEND/TERMINATE)
- lib/hosting.ts (pure validators: username derivation, domain validation, disk quota config, FPM pool config generators, DB grant SQL builder — read the comment block near "Provisioner hardening" carefully)
- lib/hosting-db.ts (the DB Studio query transport — mysql2 over an ssh2 forwardOut tunnel, authenticating as a scoped `<user>_mgr` MySQL user)
- lib/actions-hosting.ts (customer-facing server actions: order, subdomain/addon-domain creation, cron CRUD, DB creation, hostname-claim logic)
- lib/hosting-fs.ts (the file manager — should connect AS the jailed user so the OS chroot enforces boundaries)

Already CONFIRMED fixed and verified live (do not re-flag these unless you find they are NOT actually effective): DB Studio uses mysql2 protocol driver (no CLI, so no \! /source /tee meta-command escape) — I just ran a live functional test proving cross-tenant MySQL access is denied and CLI meta-commands are inert; nginx has `disable_symlinks if_not_owner` + kernel `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (fixes a symlink-to-another-tenant's-file read); MariaDB bound to 127.0.0.1 with no anonymous users; real per-tenant disk quotas enforced (verified via repquota); PAM `pam_limits.so` active in /etc/pam.d/cron with nproc soft=256/hard=400 system-wide (fixes fork-bomb DoS via cron); ModSecurity WAF is on; fail2ban + unattended-upgrades active; hostname claims are enforced via a UNIQUE column in a transaction (TOCTOU-safe); backup/restore no longer runs tenant-controlled SQL as root (dumps go to a root-only dir, restore replays only the tenant's own `_*` databases).

Your job: find anything NOT yet covered by the above. Look specifically for: PHP-FPM pool config gaps (open_basedir escapes, disable_functions completeness — can a tenant call exec/shell_exec/proc_open/pcntl_exec or similar to spawn a process outside the FPM jail?), whether the FPM pool's own user can still read other tenants' home directories via world/group-readable perms, whether app-catalog one-click installs (WordPress/Joomla/etc.) run any command as a shared/root user, whether the subdomain/addon-domain/cron server actions properly re-validate ownership (IDOR: can accountId be swapped to act on someone else's account?), and any command constructed via string interpolation that reaches a shell without being validated by the pure validators in lib/hosting.ts first.

Report findings as: file:line, the exact failure scenario (concrete steps a malicious tenant would take), severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), and your confidence. If you find nothing beyond what's already fixed, say so explicitly — don't manufacture findings. Be skeptical of your own findings: try to construct a concrete exploit path, not just "this looks risky." Report in under 600 words plus any code snippets needed to prove a real finding.

I'm checking that the recipe URL isn't tenant-controlled, so it's safe from injection since slugs are validated against a fixed catalog. Then I'm reviewing the PHP disabled functions list, confirming proc_open is blocked so proc_close isn't a concern, and checking whether assert-related functions are also covered.

Cross-tenant risk from posix_kill or posix_setuid seems minimal since the FPM pool user is unprivileged and the kernel enforces uid checks limiting signals to its own processes. I confirm imap_open is blocked, which is good since it's historically been abused for local file access or RCE via crafted mailbox parameters.

I'm also checking whether error_log could leak info by writing to arbitrary files, but open_basedir keeps it confined to the tenant's home directory, so blocking it is just extra caution. I verify open_basedir properly includes the shared PHP library path alongside the home directory without exposing other tenants' data, and the socket ownership setup (user-owned, www-data group) looks correctly scoped for nginx access without granting broader permissions.

The default listen.mode of 0660 means owner and group get read/write while others get nothing, so other tenants can't directly connect to a neighboring PHP-FPM socket even by attempting fsockopen -- unix permissions would deny the connection since they're neither the owner nor part of the www-data group.

For home directories at 711 (root:root), others can traverse but can't list contents, so a peer tenant could theoretically cd into another user's home if they knew the exact path. But the webroot itself is 2750 owned by user:www-data, meaning "other" has zero permissions there -- no execute bit means a peer can't even traverse into it, so they'd be blocked before reaching any files regardless of whether they know the filenames.

Now I want to check whether subdomain and addon domain directories under /home/{username}/subdomains/{label} and /home/{username}/domains/{domain} follow the same ownership and permission scheme, so I'm going to look at the provisioner code that creates these paths to see if it reuses the same filesystem plan or applies different modes -- and I should also check the addon domain creation logic, cron handling, and the DB studio actions for potential IDOR issues.

I notice both install tasks properly scope execution to the tenant's own user via sudo, which keeps things confined. But I'm now catching an important detail about how the cron.command field gets written, which could matter for security.

Since cron commands run as the tenant's own user regardless of their login shell, the nologin restriction (which blocks interactive SSH but allows SFTP) doesn't actually prevent arbitrary command execution through cron — a tenant could still schedule any command since cron ignores the shell restriction entirely.

Since the tenant's process runs unrestricted by PATH or open_basedir (a PHP-FPM-only limitation), cron gives them full shell capability including access to sudo or setuid binaries. This isn't a cross-tenant vector by itself, but it does mean cron effectively grants full shell access despite the nologin setup being meant to prevent that.

Right, so cron effectively gives shell-equivalent execution even though nologin blocks SSH directly—that's a real bypass of the "no shell access" control, but not necessarily a cross-tenant issue since the prompt's threat model already grants the customer full control over their own cron jobs as an assumed capability.

From there, the real question is what a customer can reach beyond their own uid: home dirs and webroots are locked down at 711/750 with proper ownership, so kernel permission enforcement should block reading peer data regardless of access vector, and root escalation would depend on unpatched SUID binaries or kernel exploits that are outside the scope of an application-level code review.

Since MariaDB now binds only to 127.0.0.1 with no anonymous users, any tenant with shell access via cron could still connect directly to that local socket with the mysql client and try arbitrary credentials, since MySQL isn't restricted per-uid at the network layer -- meaning the real barrier is credential secrecy, not process isolation.

Actually, brute-forcing another tenant's DB requires guessing a 22-char random password, which is infeasible — this is expected behavior, similar to how real cPanel handles local db access via localhost. Since cron already runs confined as the jailed user, this isn't new or something I should flag as a fresh vulnerability.

I want to shift focus to genuinely new gaps instead, like checking the WordPress/app install task where docroot download commands run via sudo as the user, pulling from a fixed recipe catalog rather than user-controlled input.

The sudo -u pattern is just root dropping privileges to run as another user, which is standard and not a vulnerability. I also want to check the Adminer install tool for a token-validated temp directory in the webroot, and look at how accountFsPlan handles subdomains and addon domains using the same web setup.

Now I'm confirming that resolveInstallTarget properly scopes by accountId, and that worker task functions consistently scope database lookups by accountId to prevent cross-account writes — findFirst queries with both id and accountId. The real question is whether lib/actions-hosting.ts verifies ownership of accountId before enqueuing tasks, since that's where a tenant could potentially pass someone else's accountId, so I need to trace through that server actions file next. I'm also checking hostingUsageSweep's disk usage commands against validated usernames, which look safe, and considering whether sandbox mode task queuing differs from the real execution path in a way that matters for security.

Since the tenant lacks write access to $home, they can't unlink or swap in a symlink for public_html or tmp, so this particular attack path seems blocked.

Since restore runs as root, this becomes a real privilege escalation vector: a tenant plants a symlink at a path within their own webroot pointing at a sensitive file like /etc/passwd, then includes that same relative path in a backup archive they control. That's not used recursively in this restore path, only applied to the webroot itself, so it's fine. The db restore step only touches the user's own dump files, and I'm now checking the backup dump step where mysqldump writes into a root-owned 700 directory that gets freshly created each run.

The tar command archives both `/home/${u}` and the root-owned dumpDir together, and by default tar doesn't dereference symlinks -- so a tenant-planted symlink pointing outside their tree would just be stored as a symlink reference rather than actually pulling in the target content.

So this backup/restore path looks safe thanks to tar's standard non-dereferencing behavior combined with the recursive chown. Now I want to double-check the restore step's file copy, which uses `cp -a`, equivalent to `cp -dR --preserve=all` -- the `-d` flag means it won't follow symlinks in the source, copying them as symlinks instead.

But I realize the real risk isn't the source side, it's whether the destination itself could already be a symlink that the tenant planted before the restore runs, since they control what's inside their home directory even though they don't own the top-level directory. The dangerous scenario for `cp` is when it copies a regular file from source onto a destination path that's already an existing symlink someone else set up in advance, since `cp` might follow that symlink and overwrite whatever it points to.

So the key question becomes whether the restore wipes `$home` clean before copying stage content into it, or whether it merely layers the stage content on top of the tenant's existing live files -- since if it's the latter, a pre-planted malicious symlink at a given path in the tenant's home would still be there when cp copies matching regular files from the stage into it.

That opens an exploit path: a tenant backs up their account while a file like `public_html/wp-config.php` is a normal regular file, then afterward deletes it and replaces it with a symlink pointing at a root-owned target like a cron file or SSH authorized_keys, so that a later restore-triggered write follows the symlink and corrupts that target instead.

I need to verify the actual `cp` behavior here: since the destination path is a symlink, GNU cp's open() call with O_CREAT|O_TRUNC would follow that symlink and overwrite whatever it points to, rather than unlinking and replacing the symlink itself — unless `--remove-destination` was explicitly passed, which it wasn't in this script. That distinction is critical to confirming whether the attack actually writes into `/etc/cron.d/malicious` or just breaks the symlink.

Actually it's even worse than I thought — even a dangling symlink works, since O_CREAT will create the file at the resolved (nonexistent) target path as long as root has write permission on that directory, which it almost always does. So an attacker pointing the symlink at a nonexistent path like /etc/cron.d/malicious lets a root-run cp create that file outright with attacker-chosen content, making this a genuine root-level arbitrary file write vulnerability in the restore path.

config.php, backs it up, then swaps it for a symlink to /etc/cron.d/evilcron, and restores — root's cp writes the malicious crontab entry there, cron executes it as root on the next tick, and the tenant gains full root privilege escalation (e.g., via SUID on bash). This is a critical finding. Let me verify the exact taskRestore code in worker/hosting.ts once more to confirm this path.

Looking at taskRestore, I see it parses the backup ID from the payload, looks up the backup record scoped to the account, validates the backup path against a strict regex requiring it live under /var/hosting-backups/, then sets up a staging directory owned by root before extracting the tarball.

Confirming my earlier concern: the restore then copies the extracted files back over the account's home directory using root permissions, meaning anything in that backup archive gets written as root into a directory the account owner can influence -- a real privilege escalation risk if the tarball's contents aren't fully trusted.

This effectively gives any tenant full root privilege escalation, since it needs no PHP execution at all — just standard SFTP access to their own webroot plus the self-service backup/restore feature that's available to every paying customer without any admin gate. This completely bypasses every other hardening measure like open_basedir, disable_functions, and chroot, because none of those matter when the attack path never touches PHP execution at all.

I'm now checking this against the already-fixed findings list, and it's clear this is a distinct, new vulnerability — the mentioned fix was about backup dumps going to a root-only directory and restore only replaying the tenant's own databases, which addresses the SQL/DB replay path, not this file-restore symlink-following path via cp. This file-copy vulnerability during restore appears completely unaddressed by that fix.

I need to be careful about which side of the cp operation follows symlinks — source or destination. Let me pin down the exact behavior: GNU cp opens the destination via a syscall that follows symlinks by default, meaning writing to a destination path that's actually a symlink will write through to whatever it points to, which is the crux of the vulnerability here.

This confirms it: GNU coreutils documents explicitly that cp's default behavior is to follow a destination symlink and overwrite its referent rather than delete-and-recreate it, unless `--remove-destination` is passed. That's a solid, well-founded confirmation of the vulnerability pattern I found in worker/hosting.ts.

Its taskRestore step's file restore command follows symlinks planted in a tenant's own webroot, letting any paying customer escalate to arbitrary root file writes -- a genuine root privilege escalation via self-service Backup+Restore, exploitable through something like /etc/cron.d. This confirms cp -a is the core vulnerability. I want to see if this same symlink-following pattern shows up elsewhere, like in taskBackup, where content might move from a tenant-writable location to a root path -- checking whether the tar archive creation step there could be similarly exploited, though creating an archive (rather than extracting one) seems less likely to be an issue.

I'm confirming tar extraction here doesn't dereference symlinks without an explicit flag, so it's safe. This is the only such copy operation, confirming it's an isolated, single-point vulnerability.

## Findings

**CRITICAL — root privilege escalation via self-service Backup/Restore (symlink-following `cp`)**

`worker/hosting.ts:1301`, in `taskRestore`:
```js
await run(conn, "restore files", `[ -d ${stage}/${u} ] && cp -a ${stage}/${u}/. ${home}/ 2>/dev/null; true`);
```

`conn` is the node's **root** SSH connection (same one used for provisioning). `${home}` is the tenant's live, currently-in-use home directory (`/home/<user>`), whose `public_html` subtree the tenant owns and can freely write into via SFTP (`accountFsPlan`: `webroot` is `2750 <user>:www-data`). GNU `cp`'s documented default behavior (absent `--remove-destination`) is: if the destination path is an existing symlink, it opens/follows that symlink and overwrites (or creates) whatever it points to, rather than replacing the link.

Concrete exploit, fully self-service, no admin involved:
1. Tenant writes a file in their own webroot, e.g. `public_html/wp-config.php`, containing attacker-chosen content — for example a crontab line: `* * * * * root chmod u+s /bin/bash`.
2. Tenant calls `createHostingBackup(accountId)` (`lib/actions-hosting.ts`, owner-gated only) to snapshot that file into a `.tar.gz`.
3. Tenant deletes that file and replaces it with a symlink they fully control the target of, e.g. `public_html/wp-config.php -> /etc/cron.d/nx` (they own `public_html`, so creating/replacing entries inside it needs no privilege beyond what they already have).
4. Tenant calls `restoreHostingBackup(accountId, backupId)` (same file, owner-gated only) on the backup from step 2.
5. The worker extracts the archive to a root-owned staging dir, then runs the `cp -a` above **as root**. It copies the *regular file* `wp-config.php` from the backup onto `${home}/public_html/wp-config.php`, which is now a symlink to `/etc/cron.d/nx`. Per `cp`'s default semantics, root's `cp` follows that symlink and writes the tenant's chosen content into `/etc/cron.d/nx`, creating the file if it doesn't exist.
6. Cron (running as root) picks up the new `/etc/cron.d/nx` entry within a minute and executes it — full root code execution. The same technique works against `/etc/passwd`, `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, a systemd unit override, `/etc/sudoers.d/*`, etc.

This completely bypasses every other control audited here (open_basedir, disable_functions, chroot, PAM limits, MySQL grants) because it never touches PHP or MySQL — it only requires the SFTP write access every paying customer already has plus the self-serve Backup/Restore feature, both confirmed unrestricted in `lib/actions-hosting.ts` (`ownedActiveAccount` is the only gate on `createHostingBackup`/`restoreHostingBackup`).

Confidence: high. `tar`/`chown -R` elsewhere in the file correctly avoid dereferencing symlinks (matches expected coreutils defaults), so this is not a general pattern bug — it's specific to this one `cp -a` invocation, which is otherwise the only cp/mv/rsync call in the file.

**Fix direction (not implemented by me, since this is a review):** never `cp` root-owned extracted content onto a live tenant-writable tree as root. Either (a) run the restore copy as the tenant's own uid (`sudo -u <user> cp -a ...`, mirroring how WP-CLI/app-install already drop privilege), which confines any symlink trickery to the tenant's own privilege level, and/or (b) use `cp -a --no-dereference` is not enough by itself — the safe pattern is `rsync -a --delete` is also unsafe the same way; instead extract-and-rename (build the new tree fully in a fresh directory, then atomically `rm -rf`+`mv` the whole `home` subtree) or strip/reject symlinks from the destination tree before copying (`find $home -type l -delete` under the tenant's own uid first, or extract with tar's `--no-same-owner` directly into place as the tenant user rather than root).

## Everything else reviewed

I read `lib/hosting.ts` (validators, `PHP_DISABLED_FUNCTIONS`, `accountFsPlan`, grant builders), the full `worker/hosting.ts` provisioner/task-queue (vhost/FPM generation, lifecycle, subdomain/addon/cron tasks, app-catalog installs, SSL sweeps), `lib/hosting-db.ts` (DB Studio transport), `lib/actions-hosting.ts` and `lib/actions-hosting-db.ts` (every customer-facing action), and `lib/hosting-fs.ts` (file manager). Beyond the `cp -a` restore bug:

- Every IDOR surface I checked (`createSubdomain`/`deleteSubdomain`, addon domain create/delete, cron CRUD, DB create/reveal/reset, plan upgrade, backup create/restore, file manager, DB Studio actions) consistently re-checks `account.userId === user.id || role === ADMIN` before acting, and every worker task re-scopes subdomain/addon/db rows by `accountId` again before touching the shell — no accountId-swap IDOR found.
- `PHP_DISABLED_FUNCTIONS` is complete against the standard shared-hosting escape set (exec family, `pcntl_*`, `putenv`, `dl`/`ffi`, `symlink`/`link`, mail family); backtick operator is covered transitively via `shell_exec`.
- FPM pool/webroot/home permission model (711/2750/700) correctly blocks a peer tenant's process from traversing into another tenant's webroot even if it knew exact paths, and FPM sockets aren't reachable across tenants (owner+www-data-group only, default 0660).
- `hostingFsTarget`/SFTP correctly connects as the jailed unix user, not root, so the OS chroot is the real boundary there.
- One-click app installs (`taskAppInstall`, `taskWordpressInstall`) download/extract via `sudo -u <tenant>`, never as root, and DB grants go through the same escaped/scoped-grant builder as everything else.
- Cron commands run as the tenant's own uid via `crontab -u`, which is an accepted, in-scope capability per the stated threat model (not a new escalation by itself).

I did not find any other new cross-tenant or privilege-escalation gap beyond the one above; I'm not re-flagging anything from the already-confirmed-fixed list.
